content: Melatonin, chemically known as 5-methoxy-N-acetyltryptamine, is a hormone present in all living organisms, ranging from algae to humans. Its levels fluctuate in a diurnal cycle. The biological effects of melatonin are mediated through its activation of melatonin receptors, as well as its role as a potent antioxidant, particularly in protecting nuclear and mitochondrial DNA from damage. In higher animals, melatonin is synthesized by pinealocytes in the pineal gland, located in the brain, as well as by the retina, lens, and gastrointestinal tract. It is derived from the amino acid tryptophan through the intermediate synthesis of serotonin, catalyzed by the enzyme 5-hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase. The production of melatonin in the pineal gland is regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which receives input from the retina regarding the daily light-dark cycle. Melatonin is also synthesized by various plants, such as rice, and ingested melatonin has been shown to reach and bind to melatonin receptors in mammalian brains. Dangerous Side Effects Asthma Research indicates that melatonin supplementation may exacerbate symptoms in patients with nocturnal asthma. A study titled Immunomodulatory Effects of Melatonin in Asthma found that even small doses of melatonin can worsen asthma symptoms by triggering the release of pro-inflammatory chemicals, such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Arthritis Animal studies suggest a potential link between melatonin and increased severity of arthritis in certain individuals. A study titled The Pineal Hormone Melatonin Exaggerates Development of Collagen-Induced Arthritis in Mice demonstrated that mice injected with melatonin during the early stages of arthritis development exhibited more severe symptoms. The findings support the hypothesis that high melatonin release from the pineal gland may enhance T-cell priming, thereby exacerbating arthritis. Testis Size In hamsters, melatonin has been associated with reduced testis size. A study titled Effects of Melatonin and 6-Methoxybenzoxazolinone on Photoperiodic Control of Testis Size in Adult Male Golden Hamsters found that melatonin significantly influenced testis size, as measured over several weeks. Distribution Melatonin produced in the pineal gland functions as an endocrine hormone, being released into the bloodstream. In contrast, melatonin synthesized in the retina and gastrointestinal tract acts as a paracrine hormone, exerting local effects. Roles Biological Clock In humans, melatonin is produced by the pineal gland, a pea-sized structure located in the center of the brain on the dorsal surface of the diencephalon. Melatonin plays a role in regulating the circadian cycle, although the central nervous system primarily controls the daily rhythms of the endocrine and paracrine systems. Melatonin production is inhibited by light and stimulated by darkness, earning it the nickname the hormone of darkness. Its secretion peaks in the middle of the night and gradually decreases during the latter half of the night. Modern artificial lighting has significantly reduced the duration of darkness exposure, potentially impacting melatonin production and contributing to higher cancer rates in night workers. Reduced melatonin levels have also been implicated in the increased incidence of certain cancers in developed countries. Antioxidant Melatonin initially evolved as an antioxidant and remains a powerful one, capable of crossing cell membranes and the blood-brain barrier. Unlike other antioxidants, melatonin does not undergo redox cycling, meaning it does not alternate between reduced and oxidized states. Once oxidized, melatonin forms stable end-products and cannot revert to its original state, earning it the designation of a terminal antioxidant. Recent research suggests that the melatonin antioxidant pathway may begin with N(1)-acetyl-N(2)-formyl-5-methoxykynuramine (AFMK) rather than the commonly excreted 6-hydroxymelatonin sulfate. AFMK and its derivatives can neutralize multiple reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), extending the antioxidant cascade to quaternary metabolites. This property is unique to melatonin and not observed in conventional antioxidants. In animal models, melatonin has been shown to prevent DNA damage caused by carcinogens and may reduce damage associated with Parkinson's disease, cardiac arrhythmias, and aging. Immune System Melatonin interacts with the immune system, although the specifics remain unclear. It acts as an immunoregulator, enhancing T-cell production and serving as an immunostimulant when combined with calcium. However, this increased immune activity may aggravate autoimmune disorders. Dreaming Many users of melatonin supplements report more vivid or frequent dreams. High doses of melatonin (50 mg) have been shown to increase REM sleep and dream activity in both narcoleptics and healthy individuals. Some psychoactive drugs, such as LSD and cocaine, also increase melatonin synthesis, suggesting a potential overlap in their mechanisms of action. Medical Applications Melatonin has shown promise in treating circadian rhythm sleep disorders, such as jet lag and delayed sleep phase syndrome. It has also been studied for its potential in treating cancer, immune disorders, cardiovascular diseases, depression, seasonal affective disorder (SAD), and sexual dysfunction. However, its effects on endogenous melatonin production and its potential to exacerbate depression and SAD require further investigation. Preventing Ischemic Damage In animal studies, melatonin has been shown to reduce tissue damage caused by ischemia in the brain and heart, although this has not been tested in humans. Learning, Memory, and Alzheimer's Disease Melatonin receptors are involved in learning and memory mechanisms in mice. Melatonin has been shown to prevent tau protein hyperphosphorylation, which can lead to neurofibrillary tangles—a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. Melatonin supplementation may also alleviate sundowning, a condition characterized by afternoon agitation in Alzheimer's patients. ADHD Melatonin has been effective in reducing sleep onset latency in ADHD patients, particularly those experiencing insomnia due to methylphenidate use. Its effects remain consistent over time, with no significant changes observed after three months of use. Fertility Melatonin supplementation in perimenopausal women has been shown to improve thyroid function, gonadotropin levels, fertility, and menstruation while preventing menopause-associated depression. However, some sources advise against melatonin use in women trying to conceive. Headaches Clinical studies suggest that melatonin supplementation is effective in preventing migraines and cluster headaches. Depression Melatonin has been shown to be effective in treating seasonal affective disorder (SAD). Other Potential Uses Preliminary studies suggest that melatonin may have potential in treating various cancers, HIV, and other viral diseases, though further research is needed. Dietary Supplement Melatonin is widely used as a natural sleep aid and is available over the counter in the United States. It is also marketed for its antioxidant properties and immune system benefits. However, many melatonin supplements contain doses far exceeding the amount needed to achieve physiological nocturnal blood levels. Smaller doses may be equally effective for improving sleep quality, and excessive doses can be counterproductive. Safety Melatonin is considered non-toxic and has minimal short-term side effects. However, melatonin derived from animal sources may carry a risk of viral contamination, which can be avoided by using synthetic melatonin. Long-term side effects remain unknown. High doses can cause hormone fluctuations, irritability, reduced blood flow, and vivid nightmares. Melatonin should not be taken with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) due to the risk of overdose. It may also exacerbate symptoms in individuals with autoimmune disorders or orthostatic intolerance. Role in Zoology In animals, melatonin regulates seasonal reproductive cycles and can suppress libido by inhibiting luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion. It also plays a role in skin color changes in some amphibians and reptiles.
